title: Chosun Expo — the front company behind the hacks
review_note: Rewritten in plain spoken English (owner feedback). Facts unchanged from the verified version (DOJ press release re-checked 2026-10-28; complaint affidavit via National Security Archive OCR copy, Dark Reading, SCMP, Wikipedia) plus NPR for North Korea calling The Interview an act of war.

scenes.label: Coders for hire, on paper
scenes.narration: [dramatically] The hackers who hit Sony and robbed a bank were exposed by Gmail. [short pause] Not by some genius trick. By ordinary email accounts, the FBI says. [curious] To see how, picture a small team of programmers for hire. They work in an office in China. They write code for paying clients, and they answer email. [short pause] On paper, their company was a normal software business. It was called Chosun Expo. [serious] But in 2018, the United States government said it was something else. [slowly] It said Chosun Expo was a cover for North Korea's hackers.

scenes.label: A quiet coder named Park
scenes.narration: [calmly] Let's go back to the start. Chosun Expo had offices in China and in North Korea. It sold the work of North Korean coders to clients in other countries. Investigators say some of those clients knew exactly who they were hiring. One of the coders was a man named Park Jin Hyok. According to the FBI, he worked for the company from at least 2002. For years, he looked like any other programmer. [short pause] He even used his real name.

visuals.query: FBI wanted poster Park Jin Hyok
visuals.at: a man named Park Jin Hyok

scenes.label: A day job in Dalian
scenes.narration: [softly] Between 2011 and 2013, Park spent time in Dalian. That's a busy port city in northeast China. There, he worked on computer projects for paying clients. He used company email accounts, including free Gmail accounts. That's normal. Lots of small businesses use Gmail. [short pause] But the FBI says Chosun Expo had a second boss. It was linked to a hacking unit called Lab 110. The US says Lab 110 is part of North Korea's military spy service.

scenes.label: The hackers with a nickname
scenes.narration: [curious] Security experts had been chasing a group of hackers for years. They didn't know their real names. So they gave them a nickname, the Lazarus Group. [serious] Prosecutors say Park was part of that group. By 2014, the FBI says, he seemed to be back home in North Korea. That same year, a Hollywood comedy was about to come out. It was called The Interview. In the story, two Americans are sent to kill Kim Jong Un. [short pause] North Korea's government called the movie an act of war.

scenes.label: Bait for the actors
scenes.narration: [cautiously] In September 2014, strange Facebook messages started to show up. One account used the names Watson Henny and John Mogabe. Another was called Andoson David. They posted links aimed at actors in The Interview. [short pause] The links were bait. Click one, and you could get malware. Malware is just a program built to break into a computer, or damage it. Nobody on the outside knew it yet. [slowly] But someone was knocking on Sony's door.

scenes.label: Hacked by GOP
scenes.narration: [dramatically] Then came November. On November 21, 2014, Sony bosses got an email from someone calling himself Frank David. It demanded money. Three days later, on November 24, Sony computers lit up with a message. It said, Hacked by GOP. The letters stood for Guardians of Peace. [breathless] Sony had to cut off nearly 8,000 computers to stop the damage. Private files spilled onto the internet. Even a new movie, Annie, leaked online before it came out.

scenes.label: $81 million walks out
scenes.narration: [serious] Hollywood was only the start. Just over a year later, the target was money. In February 2016, hackers broke into Bangladesh Bank. That's the country's central bank, like America's Federal Reserve. They sent fake payment orders through SWIFT. SWIFT is the system banks use to send money to each other across borders. [short pause] About $81 million got away. The FBI called it the biggest successful cyber-theft from a bank so far. [ominously] And they wanted more.

scenes.label: Knocking at Lockheed Martin
scenes.narration: [cautiously] Prosecutors say the same group tried to steal at least $1 billion from other banks. Then they turned to America's defense industry. In 2016 and 2017, they sent spear-phishing emails to US defense companies, including Lockheed Martin. Spear-phishing means a fake email made for one person, to trick them into clicking. Some emails were about a missile defense system that Lockheed builds. [short pause] This time, the trick failed. Lockheed's doors stayed shut.

scenes.label: WannaCry hits the world
scenes.narration: [urgently] Then, in May 2017, came the attack almost everyone heard about. It was called WannaCry. It was ransomware. That's a program that locks your files and demands money to unlock them. It spread by itself, from computer to computer. Hundreds of thousands of machines were hit around the world. [sad] In Britain, it hit the National Health Service, the country's public health system. Thousands of hospital appointments were canceled. [pause] Who was behind it? The FBI had been digging for years.

visuals.at: the attack almost everyone heard about

scenes.label: The clue in the inbox
scenes.narration: [curious] So how do you catch a hacker from one of the most secretive countries on Earth? [short pause] In this case, the answer was email. Remember those free Gmail accounts Chosun Expo used for its normal business? Some were in Park's real name. Agents found that one of them was tied to a second Gmail account with a very similar name. [serious] And that second account was busy. It was used to send fake emails, to study targets, and to research hacking.

scenes.label: Who was Kim Hyon Woo?
scenes.narration: [serious] That second account used a name, Kim Hyon Woo. The FBI says it was likely a fake name, a cover. Kim Hyon Woo accounts were used to set up other email and social media accounts. Some of those were used against Sony and Bangladesh Bank. Remember the Andoson David Facebook account that sent bait to the actors? [short pause] The FBI says it was set up with one of those same email addresses. [slowly] A single thread now ran from the quiet coder to the attacks.

visuals.at: one of those same email addresses

scenes.label: Too many fingerprints
scenes.narration: [calmly] Email wasn't the only clue. Investigators also matched fake names used again and again. They found the same pieces of code showing up in different attacks. They traced logins back to internet addresses in North Korea and China. [short pause] Eric Chien of the security company Symantec said Park mixed his normal work with his government work. And because he used American email services, US search warrants could reach those accounts. [reflective] Another expert, Priscilla Moriuchi, said the case was built on all the mistakes he made.

visuals.query: United States District Court Los Angeles

scenes.label: Charged, then denied
scenes.narration: [serious] On June 8, 2018, prosecutors filed a criminal complaint in Los Angeles. It stayed secret for three months. Then, on September 6, 2018, the charges went public. Park was charged with conspiracy to commit computer fraud and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The second charge alone carries up to 20 years in prison. That same day, the US Treasury put money sanctions on Park and on Chosun Expo. [surprised] And North Korea's answer? It said Park Jin Hyok doesn't even exist.

visuals.at: a criminal complaint in Los Angeles

visuals.query: Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice Building

scenes.label: Undone by an inbox
scenes.narration: [softly] As far as the public knows, Park Jin Hyok has never been arrested. He is still on the FBI's wanted list. The charges have never been tested in court, so they are still only accusations. [short pause] But the case put a real company, and a real face, behind years of attacks. Behind the code names were people with day jobs. [slowly] And what gave them away was the most ordinary thing in any office… an email account. [pause] If you like true stories like this, subscribe to Breach Uncovered.

facts.claim: The complaint against Park Jin Hyok was filed June 8, 2018 in Los Angeles federal court and announced September 6, 2018.

Chosun Expo Joint Venture (Korea Expo Joint Venture) is described as a North Korean government front company with offices in China and the DPRK, affiliated with Lab 110, a component of DPRK military intelligence.
Affiant is FBI Special Agent Nathan P. Shields, Los Angeles Field Office; the affidavit's conclusion is at paragraph 171.
Chosun Expo stationed programmers abroad, including in Dalian, China, doing programming and IT projects for paying clients, some of whom knew they were hiring North Koreans.
Park worked for Chosun Expo from at least 2002, was in China for at least part of 2011–2013, and appears to have returned to North Korea by 2014; Chosun Expo accounts were in his true name.

In September 2014 a Facebook account using the names Watson Henny / John Mogabe posted malware links to actors in The Interview; an 'Andoson David' Facebook account, subscribed with the Kim Hyon Woo Gmail account, did the same.

A 'Frank David' email on November 21, 2014 demanded compensation from Sony; on November 24 workstations displayed 'Hacked by #GOP'; Sony disconnected 7,500 to 8,000 workstations; a pre-release copy of Annie was posted online.

About $81 million was stolen from Bangladesh Bank in February 2016 via fraudulent SWIFT messages; the affidavit calls it the largest successful cyber-theft from a financial institution to date; attempted losses 2015–2018 were well over $1 billion.
Spear-phishing of US defense contractors including Lockheed Martin in 2016–2017 was unsuccessful; a subject using a North Korean IP address researched and messaged Lockheed personnel.
The complaint alleges the same subjects authored WannaCry 2.0 (May 2017), which infected hundreds of thousands of computers, including in the Central District of California.
WannaCry hit the UK's NHS and thousands of appointments were canceled.

Chosun Expo used free email services for routine business; one Chosun Expo Gmail account was linked to a second with a similar handle used for spear-phishing, reconnaissance and hacking research; 'Kim Hyon Woo' was 'likely an alias or cover name'.
Investigators linked the attacks through email and social media accounts, aliases, malware collector accounts, common code libraries, proxy services and IP addresses.
A Brambul worm collector account was accessed from a North Korean IP address in 2017.

Eric Chien (Symantec) cited 'a lack of opsec' and said Park 'cross-contaminated' legitimate and government work; Priscilla Moriuchi (Recorded Future): investigators 'were able to build this case against him based on all the mistakes he made'; free US email exposed accounts to US search warrants.

Charges: conspiracy to commit computer fraud and abuse (max 5 years) and conspiracy to commit wire fraud (max 20 years); Treasury OFAC sanctioned Park and KEJV under E.O. 13722; Demers: 'The scale and scope of the cyber-crimes alleged by the Complaint is staggering'.
Park is on the FBI wanted list; North Korea denies that Park exists.
The company used free email services such as Gmail for routine business and for phishing; clues in Gmail helped investigators.
In June 2014 North Korea's government (via KCNA/foreign ministry) called The Interview, a comedy about a plot to kill Kim Jong Un, an 'act of war'.
Some spear-phishing emails to Lockheed Martin referenced THAAD, the missile defense system for which Lockheed is prime contractor; the attempts were not successful.
WannaCry spread itself from computer to computer (worm-like ransomware) and hit hundreds of thousands of computers, significantly impacting the UK's NHS.

seo.youtube_title: How the FBI Unmasked a North Korean Hacker: The Chosun Expo Story
seo.youtube_description:
How the FBI unmasked a North Korean hacker: the true story of Chosun Expo, the "software company" the US says was a cover for North Korea's hackers.
One coder for hire, Park Jin Hyok, is charged over the Sony Pictures hack, the $81 million Bangladesh Bank theft and WannaCry. What gave him away? Gmail.

On paper, Chosun Expo was a normal company. It had offices in China and North Korea and sold the work of North Korean programmers to paying clients. One of them, Park Jin Hyok, worked in Dalian, China, using his real name. But the FBI says the company was tied to Lab 110, a hacking unit in North Korea's military spy service, and to the hackers known as the Lazarus Group.

Prosecutors say the same group sent bait to actors in The Interview, wiped Sony computers in 2014, stole $81 million from Bangladesh Bank in 2016, went after Lockheed Martin and released WannaCry in 2017. The case cracked because of ordinary email accounts that linked Park's real name to a fake one, Kim Hyon Woo. He was charged in 2018 and sanctioned by the US Treasury. He has never been arrested, and the charges are still accusations.
